title: SpyDER
summary: A local-first Python camera control room that combines concurrent monitoring, computer vision, visual workflows, event history and tiled recording without a cloud video-processing backend.

problem: Monitoring multiple cameras becomes fragmented when capture, device tuning, model inference, recording and alerts live in separate tools. Opening duplicate captures can create contention, while cloud inference introduces a remote dependency for private video.
purpose: I set out to build an installable local application where camera feeds, computer vision and user-defined detection actions share one runtime, with a browser interface and a separate static showcase that processes supported demo features on the visitor's device.
keyFeatures: Responsive multi-camera Control Room and fullscreen tiled viewing, with per-camera controls and capture/recording actions.
MOG2 motion analysis, contours, connected components, tracking, ROI selection and preview-before-apply controls.
Visual workflows with camera/model inputs, detection and classification, multi-connection branches, filters, zones, cooldowns and restricted Python/JavaScript code nodes.
Inline workflow previews that preserve the live canvas through cosmetic graph changes and zooming.
Local model upload/registration, metadata and class inspection, reusable model nodes and reference-aware removal.
Persistent motion/workflow events with naming patterns, capture or timed-clip attachments, search/filter/group controls, rename and bulk export/deletion.
One dynamically tiled local recording, frame captures and inline media viewing with a compatibility preview for unsupported browser codecs.
Camera tuning profiles, persisted focus policy, local diagnostics and configurable output folders with access to previous media.
role: I led the product design and implementation of the local camera/CV architecture, browser interface, workflow interactions, model integration, recording and event storage, packaging, and the static showcase boundary.
technicalHighlights: Per-camera workers and bounded latest-frame scheduling avoid an unbounded queue when inference is slower than capture.
Live views, workflow previews and recordings reuse the camera worker rather than opening a separate device capture for every view.
Graph validation and explicit activation separate editable workflows from active camera pipelines; preview invalidation follows only its upstream processing branch.
Optional face classification uses confidence margins and consecutive confirmations to reduce switching, while exposing the limitations of closed-set identity decisions.
Timed event clips track recording-session ownership so manual or other workflow control is not stopped by an old attachment timer.
Package-resource asset loading and stable data paths support installed execution outside the checkout; media output changes retain earlier catalogs.
The exported static showcase keeps native Python workflow controls unavailable and uses browser-local generated feeds, cameras, files and recording.

challengesAndSolutions.challenge: Multiple views and expensive inference can contend for a camera or display stale queued results.
challengesAndSolutions.solution: Use one capture owner per configured source, bounded latest-frame buffers and independent processing schedules.

challengesAndSolutions.challenge: Dragging graph nodes and changing unrelated settings used to interrupt live workflow previews.
challengesAndSolutions.solution: Base preview invalidation on upstream processing dependencies and preserve the existing preview canvas during cosmetic edits and zoom.

challengesAndSolutions.challenge: Face classifications can flicker between classes on consecutive results.
challengesAndSolutions.solution: Add confidence-margin checks and consecutive-result confirmation, with separate confirmation thresholds for identity switches.

challengesAndSolutions.challenge: A timed event recording can outlive the action that started it and accidentally stop another recording.
challengesAndSolutions.solution: Track the recorder session and ownership transfers, and stop only an unchanged event-owned session.

challengesAndSolutions.challenge: A static cloud demo cannot run the local Python inference stack.
challengesAndSolutions.solution: Export a browser-only interface with local media processing and explicit native-only boundaries instead of proxying video to a cloud backend.

resultsImpact: Brings camera monitoring, CV-driven actions and local evidence review into one installable prototype without requiring cloud video processing.
Supports a complete event-to-capture/clip workflow, with persistent metadata, local playback and exportable evidence references.
Demonstrates a static-hostable camera wall while keeping native inference and persistent local-server features clearly separated.

Provides synthetic regression coverage for camera lifecycle, model adapters, workflow behavior, event storage and installed-package resources; target hardware and real models still need separate validation.
lessonsLearned: Local-first design changes the architecture: the browser, Python runtime and static showcase need explicit capability boundaries.
Freshness, backpressure and capture ownership matter as much as model integration in a concurrent camera application.
Stable classification output is not proof of correct identification or reliable unknown-person rejection.
Package installation, resource paths and server lifecycle are part of the product experience, including safe transitions between editable and wheel installations.
Synthetic fixtures make regressions reproducible, but camera drivers, codecs, models and hardware capacity require real-device checks.
